lead: The engine takes chemical energy in with the fuel and turns part of it into work at the shaft. The rest leaves as heat, and it must go somewhere: into the cooling water, up the exhaust pipe, or out through the block by radiation and convection. A heat balance is a sheet that lists these streams in kW and as a percentage of the fuel power, and shows that they add up. It is how a test cell answers the question 'where did the fuel money go?', and it is how radiators and exhaust heat recovery equipment are sized.
prereq: You need: fuel power and brake thermal efficiency from 5.1, and brake power and fuel flow measurement from 5.3.

sections.h3: The sheet, and why it must close

blocks.text: Chemical energy enters the engine at one rate and leaves at several. The rate at which the fuel brings energy in is the fuel power:

blocks.where: P_f is the fuel power in kW, m_f is the fuel mass flow in kg/h, CV is the calorific value of the fuel in MJ/kg, and 3.6 converts kg/h × MJ/kg into kW.

blocks.text: On the output side there are four streams: brake power P_b at the shaft, heat to the cooling water P_c, heat carried away by the exhaust gas P_e, and the rest P_u, which covers radiation, convection, heat to the lubricating oil and any fuel that did not burn completely. Energy is conserved, so:

blocks.where: P_f is fuel power, P_b is brake power, P_c is heat to cooling water, P_e is heat in the exhaust gas, and P_u is the unaccounted remainder, all in kW.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach the heat balance as a full topic, but industry draws one for every new engine. Each term is then also written as a percentage of P_f.
Brake power comes from the dynamometer (see 5.2). The cooling water term comes from the water itself:

blocks.where: m_w is the cooling water mass flow in kg/s, c_pw is the specific heat of water, 4.18 kJ/kgK, and ΔT_w is the rise in water temperature across the jacket in K.

blocks.text: The exhaust term is the sensible heat in the gas above ambient:

blocks.where: m_g is the exhaust gas mass flow in kg/s, c_pg is about 1.05 kJ/kgK for exhaust gas, and ΔT_g is the exhaust temperature minus the ambient air temperature in K.

items: Water flow by rotameter, or by filling a bucket for a measured time; water temperatures by thermometers at the jacket inlet and outlet.
Exhaust gas flow is air flow plus fuel flow, m_g = m_a + m_f, both measured as in 5.3. Using air alone understates P_e.

A gas calorimeter checks the exhaust figure: it cools the gas and measures the heat given up, which includes the latent heat of the water vapour. That is why it reads slightly higher than m_g × c_pg × ΔT_g.
P_u is not measured. It is P_f minus the other three terms.

blocks.text: Two rules keep the sheet honest. First, every percentage is taken on P_f, never on P_b. Second, all four terms must be in the same unit before they are added; kW throughout is easiest, so a figure in kJ/h must be divided by 3600 first.

Draw the sheet as a bar or a divided block: one long bar of 100 % cut into four pieces, largest first. A pie chart with four thin slices is hard to read at a glance; a bar shows at once that the exhaust carries more than half the fuel energy in the worked example below.

The unaccounted term shrinks as the engine gets hotter. A cold engine stores heat in its metal and oil, and that stored heat lands in P_u. Once the engine holds a steady temperature, the storage stops and P_u falls to a small radiation and convection figure.

figure.caption: Fuel power of 35 kW splits into brake power, cooling water, exhaust and a small unaccounted term. The exhaust carries more than half of the fuel energy.

spec.title: Heat balance of the worked example
spec.aria: Block diagram of a heat balance: 35 kW of fuel energy leaves as 10 kW brake power, 5.02 kW to cooling water, 18.9 kW in the exhaust and 1.08 kW unaccounted.

examples.question: An engine burns 3.0 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 42 MJ/kg and delivers 10 kW at the brake. Cooling water flows at 6 kg/min and rises 12 °C across the jacket. Exhaust gas flows at 0.045 kg/s with c_p = 1.05 kJ/kgK and leaves 400 K above ambient. Draw up the heat balance in kW and in percent.
steps: Cooling water heat: P_c = m_w × c_pw × ΔT_w = 0.1 × 4.18 × 12 = 5.02 kW.
Exhaust heat: P_e = m_g × c_pg × ΔT_g = 0.045 × 1.05 × 400 = 18.9 kW.
Unaccounted: P_u = P_f − P_b − P_c − P_e = 35.0 − 10 − 5.02 − 18.9 = 1.08 kW.
Percentages of fuel power: brake 10/35.0 = 28.6 %; cooling 5.02/35.0 = 14.3 %; exhaust 18.9/35.0 = 54.0 %; unaccounted 1.08/35.0 = 3.1 %.
Check: 28.6 + 14.3 + 54.0 + 3.1 = 100.0 %, so the sheet closes on fuel power.
examples.answer: Fuel power 35.0 kW splits into 10 kW brake (28.6 %), 5.02 kW to cooling water (14.3 %), 18.9 kW in the exhaust (54.0 %) and 1.08 kW unaccounted (3.1 %).
examples.check:
mf = 3.0
CV = 42.0
bp = 10.0
mw = 6.0
cpw = 4.18
dTw = 12.0
mg = 0.045
cpg = 1.05
dTg = 400.0
pf = mf * CV / 3.6
pc = (mw / 60.0) * cpw * dTw
pe = mg * cpg * dTg
pu = pf - bp - pc - pe
print(round(pf, 2))
print(round(pc, 2))
print(round(pe, 2))
print(round(pu, 2))
print(round(100 * bp / pf, 1))
print(round(100 * pc / pf, 1))
print(round(100 * pe / pf, 1))
print(round(100 * pu / pf, 1))

traps: The sheet closes on fuel power, not on brake power. Percentages taken on 10 kW would give 100 % for the brake and nonsense for the rest.
Exhaust mass flow is air plus fuel, m_a + m_f, not air alone; using air alone loses the fuel mass and understates the exhaust heat.
Never mix units on one sheet: kW, kJ/h and kcal/min must all be converted to a single unit before adding.
Use the temperature rise, not the absolute temperature: ΔT_g is exhaust minus ambient, and ΔT_w is outlet minus inlet. A rise of 12 K is the same as a rise of 12 °C.
Mass flows must be in kg/s before multiplying by c_p × ΔT: divide kg/h by 3600 and kg/min by 60.

quiz.q: Name the four output terms of an engine heat balance.
quiz.a: Brake power, heat to cooling water, heat carried by the exhaust gas, and the unaccounted term (radiation, convection, oil cooler, incomplete combustion).

quiz.q: Which term of the heat balance is not measured, and how is it obtained?
quiz.a: The unaccounted term. It is fuel power minus brake power, cooling water heat and exhaust heat.

quiz.q: Why are the percentages of a heat balance taken on fuel power and not on brake power?
quiz.a: Fuel power is the total energy entering the engine, so every output is a fraction of that one input. Dividing by brake power would make the brake term 100 % and the fractions would no longer describe the fuel energy, and would not add to 100 %.

quiz.q: An engine uses 4.0 kg/h of fuel of calorific value 43 MJ/kg and gives 12 kW at the brake. Cooling water flows at 8 kg/min with a 10 °C rise; exhaust gas flows at 0.05 kg/s with c_p = 1.05 kJ/kgK and a 380 K rise. Find the unaccounted heat in kW and as a percentage of fuel power.
Convert a fuel flow of 3.0 kg/h and a cooling water flow of 6 kg/min into the units used in c_p × ΔT formulas.
Why does the unaccounted term fall as the engine reaches steady hot condition?
quiz.a: A cold engine absorbs heat into its metal, oil and coolant bulk, and that stored heat appears in the remainder. At steady temperature no more heat is stored, so the remainder reduces to radiation, convection and small losses.

quiz.q: A gas calorimeter on the exhaust reads more heat than m_g × c_pg × ΔT_g. Explain.
quiz.a: The c_p × ΔT calculation gives only sensible heat above ambient. The calorimeter cools the gas further and condenses the water vapour, so its reading also includes the latent heat of condensation of the water formed by burning the hydrogen in the fuel.

quiz.q: Why is the heat balance drawn as a bar or a divided block rather than a pie chart?
quiz.a: Four thin slices of a pie are hard to compare at a glance; a single bar cut into four parts shows at once that the exhaust is the largest stream and how the others compare with it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Heat balances are the starting point for waste heat recovery: organic Rankine cycles, turbo-compounding and thermoelectric generators all feed on the exhaust term. The same sheet sizes radiators and decides fan power. Research engines now add a fifth stream, unburnt fuel and CO in the exhaust, measured with gas analysers. Search 'engine heat balance sheet', 'exhaust energy recovery Rankine cycle' and 'turbo compounding' to go further.
